definition: The quality of being exact and careful, with no small errors or vague details.
example: The watchmaker worked with such precision that every tiny gear turned smoothly against the next.
nuance: Precision is about exact, consistent detail, while accuracy is about being correct; a measurement can be precise yet still wrong.
prompt: A carpenter is building cabinets that must fit into a narrow alcove.
options: She measured each panel with precision, so the cabinets slid into place with no gaps.
She cut the panels with precision, eyeballing each line and leaving gaps an inch wide.
She gave precision to her partner's design, letting it go first because he was senior.
After weeks of doubt, the carpenter finally made a precision to paint the cabinets white.
reasons: Careful, exact measuring that produces a perfect fit is exactly what the word describes.
Guessing at lines and leaving big gaps is sloppiness, the reverse of exactness.
This confuses the word with precedence, which means priority or going first.
This mixes the word up with decision; one cannot make a precision about a choice.

practice.prompt: A scientist writes up the results of a lab experiment.
options: Before running the test, the scientist asked the lab director for precision to use the microscope.
The lab assistant added precision to the group meeting by chatting about his weekend hiking trip.
Her report listed each temperature to a tenth of a degree, a level of precision the reviewers praised.
The report showed great precision because every reading was rounded to the nearest hundred degrees.
reasons: This confuses the word with permission; exactness is not something you request access with.
Casual small talk has nothing to do with being exact or careful.
Reporting fine-grained, exact figures shows careful attention to detail.
Rounding off so heavily throws away detail, which makes the results less exact, not more.
